title: Digital Nomad Visa: 11 Countries That Welcome Remote Workers | Grey
summary: A practical guide to the 11 best digital nomad visas in 2026. Requirements, costs, and how long you can stay. Find the right one for you.
body_markdown:
With more countries now recognising the importance of digital nomads to the local economy and tourism, many have introduced a Visa category to attract more digital nomads. A digital nomad visa lets remote workers live legally in a foreign country while earning income from clients or employers elsewhere. More than 50 countries now offer them, with income requirements ranging from $1,500 to $3,500 per month.


But not all digital nomad visas are equally attractive. Some require very high monthly income thresholds that exclude many freelancers. Others come with complicated tax obligations, expensive healthcare requirements, or difficult renewal processes. A country may look attractive on Instagram but become frustrating in practice if internet reliability is poor, banking is difficult, or the cost of living is higher than expected.


This guide covers 11 of the best countries offering digital nomad visas in 2026, including visa requirements, minimum income thresholds, costs, taxes, internet quality, banking access, and what daily life is actually like for remote workers living there.


## What is a digital nomad visa and who qualifies?


A digital nomad visa is a specific immigration category created for remote workers, distinct from both a standard tourist visa and a traditional work permit. A tourist visa generally does not authorise any income-generating activity, even remote work for a foreign employer, while a traditional work permit ties you to local employment with a company based in that country. A digital nomad visa sits between the two: it explicitly authorises you to live in the country while earning income from sources outside it.


The eligibility requirements share a common pattern across most countries that offer one. You must demonstrate remote income, either as an employee of a company based outside the country or as a freelancer with clients based abroad. Most programmes set a minimum monthly or annual income threshold, ranging from roughly $1,500 to $3,500 per month depending on the country's cost of living. Valid health insurance covering your stay is almost universally required. A clean criminal record is standard. Some programmes also require proof of accommodation before or shortly after arrival.


The visas vary considerably in duration, from six months to multiple years, and in whether they offer a pathway toward permanent residency. Understanding these differences before choosing where to apply saves significant time and cost.


## 11 countries with digital nomad visas


In no specific order, here are 11 countries with great digital nomad visas and the peculiarity of each option.


### 1. Portugal


**Visa name:** D8 Digital Nomad Visa


**Minimum monthly income:** Approximately €3,680/$3,850 (four times the Portuguese minimum wage)


**Application cost:** Approximately €90 to €180 depending on consulate


**Maximum stay:** One year initially, renewable up to five years, with a pathway to permanent residency


**Standout benefit:** Long-term residency pathway within the EU and Schengen Area access


**Banking/financial note:** Opening a Portuguese bank account requires a NIF (tax identification number), obtainable as a non-resident before arrival


### 2. Spain


**Visa name:** Digital Nomad Visa


**Minimum monthly income:** Approximately €2,849/$3,050 (200% of Spain's minimum wage)


**Application cost:** Approximately €75 to €100 plus consular fees


**Maximum stay:** One year initially, renewable up to five years total


**Standout benefit:** Access to the broader Schengen Area and a clear five-year residency runway


**Banking/financial note:** A NIE (foreigner identification number) is required for local bank accounts


### 3. Germany


**Visa name:** Freiberufler (Freelance) Visa


**Minimum monthly income:** No fixed minimum, but applicants typically show €750 to €1,000 per month in client income or contracts


**Application cost:** €75 consular fee, plus €100 for Chamber of Commerce business plan review if applicable


**Maximum stay:** Up to three years initially, renewable, with a path to permanent residency after five years


**Standout benefit:** No fixed income threshold and the ability to work in recognised liberal professions such as design, writing, and consulting


**Banking/financial note:** A German bank account is not required for the initial visa application but is advisable once relocated. See our full[Germany digital nomad visa guide](https://grey.co/blog/germany-digital-nomad-visa) for the complete application process.


### 4. Costa Rica


**Visa name:** Rentista/Digital Nomad Visa


**Minimum monthly income:** $3,000 for an individual, $4,000 for a family


**Application cost:** Approximately $100 to $200 depending on processing route


**Maximum stay:** One year, renewable for an additional year


**Standout benefit:** Tax exemption on foreign-sourced income and import tax exemptions on personal equipment such as laptops


**Banking/financial note:** Local bank accounts require legal residency status and considerable documentation


### 5. Thailand


**Visa name:** Destination Thailand Visa (DTV)


**Minimum monthly income:** No fixed monthly threshold, but applicants must show 500,000 THB (approximately $14,000) in available funds


**Application cost:** 10,000 THB (approximately $280)


**Maximum stay:** Five-year multi-entry validity, with 180-day stays per entry


**Standout benefit:** Long multi-entry validity without needing to reapply annually


**Banking/financial note:** Opening a local Thai bank account requires a long-stay visa and can involve a lengthy in-branch process


### 6. Estonia


**Visa name:** Digital Nomad Visa


**Minimum monthly income:** €4,500


**Application cost:** Approximately €80 to €100 depending on nationality


**Maximum stay:** Up to one year, non-renewable within Estonia


**Standout benefit:** World's first digital nomad visa, with full Schengen Area access during the stay


**Banking/financial note:** A local Estonian bank account requires residency status. See our full[Estonia digital nomad visa guide](https://grey.co/blog/estonia-digital-nomad-visa) for the complete process.


### 7. Malaysia


**Visa name:** DE Rantau Nomad Pass


**Minimum monthly income:** $2,000/month (tech and digital professionals); $5,000/month equivalent (non-tech professionals)


**Application cost:** Approximately RM 1,000 (around $252) for the principal applicant


**Maximum stay:** 12 months, renewable once for a total of 24 months


**Standout benefit:** No Malaysian tax on foreign-sourced income, and a fully online application process


**Banking/financial note:** Opening a local bank account requires the DE Rantau pass and is relatively straightforward once the pass is issued. See our[Malaysia DE Rantau guide](https://grey.co/blog/malaysia-digital-nomad-visa) for full details.


### 8. Greece


**Visa name:** Digital Nomad Visa


**Minimum monthly income:** €3,500 after taxes (with an additional 20% for a spouse and 15% per child)


**Application cost:** €75 consular fee


**Maximum stay:** One year, renewable for an additional two years via residence permit


**Standout benefit:** A 50% income tax reduction for the first seven years for those who become Greek tax residents.


**Banking/financial note:** A Greek tax number (AFM) is needed for most financial activity, including opening a bank account.


#### 9. Georgia


**Visa name:** Standard visa-free entry (effectively functioning as a digital nomad visa for most nationalities); D2 visa for those requiring formal status.


**Minimum monthly income:** Approximately $2,000 or $24,000 in savings (for the D2 visa route).


**Application cost:** Free for visa-free entry; approximately $20 for the D2 visa.


**Maximum stay:** Up to 365 days.


**Standout benefit:** No visa application required at all for most nationalities, and one of the lowest costs of living among nomad destinations.


**Banking/financial note:** Georgia is notably accessible for foreigners opening local bank accounts, often completed in a single visit. See our full[Georgia Remoteli programme guide](https://grey.co/blog/georgia-digital-nomad-visa) for the complete picture.


#### 10. Indonesia (Bali)


**Visa name:** E33G Remote Worker Visa


**Minimum monthly income:** $60,000 per year minimum


**Application cost:** IDR 7,000,000 (approximately $430), plus agent fees typically bringing the total to $600 to $1,000


**Maximum stay:** 12 months, non-extendable


**Standout benefit:** The only Indonesian visa category that explicitly authorises remote work for a foreign employer


**Banking/financial note:** Foreign card withdrawal fees apply at most ATMs; local accounts are difficult to access for short-stay visitors. See our[Bali digital nomad visa guide](https://grey.co/blog/bali-digital-nomad-visa) for the full picture, including why most nomads still use tourist or social visas in practice.


#### 11. Mexico


**Visa name:** Temporary Resident Visa (no dedicated digital nomad category, but functions as the standard nomad pathway)


**Minimum monthly income:** Approximately $2,600 per month from foreign sources, or savings equivalent


**Application cost:** Approximately $50 to $60 for the visa, plus residency card fees on arrival


**Maximum stay:** One to four years depending on the specific permit issued


**Standout benefit:** 180 days visa-free for most Western passport holders before any visa is even needed, and close time-zone alignment with US clients


**Banking/financial note:** Local bank accounts require a *Temporal* or *Permanente* residency card. See our[Mexico Temporary Resident Visa guide](https://grey.co/blog/mexico-digital-nomad-visa) for full requirements.


## How to manage your money as a digital nomad


Every digital nomad visa helps digital nomads come into the country, settle down, and work with international clients. One thing the visa doesn’t quite solve is how you manage your finances as a digital nomad in a new country. It is important to plan for how your income gets to you and how you spend it once you arrive a new country, because this is where most new nomads lose money without realising it.


Like most digital nomads, you might earn in USD, GBP, or EUR but have to spend in a different local currency. If that income is sent via international wire to a local bank account, it must go through one or more correspondent banks. Each of these banks will deduct a handling fee. Then your local receiving bank converts the USD, EUR, or GBP at their own conversion rate, often 1% to 3% below the mid-market rate. Most of the time, you cannot even be sure how much you are receiving at the end of the day. Then, when you spend locally using a standard foreign debit card, a foreign transaction fee of 1.5% to 3% applies to every single purchase.

A US client pays via ACH to a real US routing number. A UK client pays via Faster Payments to a real UK sort code. A European client or employer pays via SEPA. The full amount arrives without correspondent bank deductions.


For spending, the[Grey virtual debit card](https://grey.co/cards) connects directly to your foreign currency balances and is accepted wherever Visa is supported internationally, without adding a foreign transaction fee on top for purchases in the card’s native currency. ### How to choose the right digital nomad visa


The right visa for you depends more on four practical factors than on the country's reputation or scenery.


- **Income level.** If your monthly income sits between $1,500 and $2,500, Georgia (visa-free or D2), Malaysia's tech-tier DE Rantau, and Mexico's Temporary Resident Visa are accessible. If your income is above $3,000 per month, Portugal, Spain, Estonia, Greece, and Costa Rica all open up.
- **Preferred region.** Portugal, Spain, Germany, Estonia, and Greece keep you within or near the Schengen Area, enabling easy regional travel. Malaysia, Thailand, and Indonesia suit Asia-Pacific time zones. Costa Rica, Mexico, and Georgia each offer distinct regional advantages depending on which clients you serve.
- **Tax implications.** Georgia's 1% flat rate for registered Individual Entrepreneurs and Malaysia's exemption on foreign-sourced income are among the most favourable. Greece offers a meaningful tax reduction for new residents. Portugal and Spain have more standard tax exposure once you become a tax resident, which typically happens after 183 days.
- **Length of stay needed.** For a short-term trial of nomad life, Georgia's visa-free entry or Thailand's DTV with its flexible multi-entry structure requires the least commitment. For those planning multi-year relocation, Portugal's five-year renewable pathway and Germany's freelance permit, which counts toward permanent residency, are the strongest options.


## Frequently asked questions


### **Can I work remotely on a tourist visa?**


In most countries, this exists in a legal grey area. Tourist visas are generally designed for leisure travel and do not explicitly authorise income-generating work, even for a foreign employer. Some countries tolerate this in practice; others, including Indonesia, have significantly increased enforcement in recent years. A dedicated digital nomad visa removes this ambiguity entirely and is the safer route for any extended stay.


### **How much income do I need for a digital nomad visa?**


Thresholds vary from roughly $1,500 to $3,500 per month depending on the country and its cost of living. Lower-cost destinations like Georgia, Malaysia, and Mexico set lower or more flexible thresholds. Higher-cost European destinations like Spain, Portugal, and Greece require higher monthly income to reflect local living costs.


### **Do digital nomad visas lead to residency?**


Some do, some do not. Portugal's D8 visa and Germany's Freiberufler permit both count toward permanent residency after a defined period. Estonia's and Indonesia's nomad visas are explicitly non-renewable within the country and do not lead toward residency. Confirm the specific residency pathway, or lack of one, before choosing a country if long-term settlement is your goal.


### **Which country has the easiest digital nomad visa to get?**


Georgia is the most accessible in practical terms. Most nationalities require no visa application at all for a stay of up to 365 days. For those seeking a formal visa with minimal complexity, Germany's Freiberufler visa has no fixed minimum income threshold, making it more accessible to those with variable or lower freelance income than in countries with strict income floors.


### **Do I pay tax on a digital nomad visa?**


This depends heavily on how long you stay and the specific country's tax residency rules. Most countries trigger tax residency after 183 days within a 12-month period. Below that threshold, most nomads remain taxed only in their home country. Above it, the destination country's tax rules apply, which vary significantly: Georgia and Malaysia offer notably favourable structures for foreign income, while Portugal and Spain apply more standard tax rates once residency is triggered. Always verify your specific position with a cross-border tax adviser.
